genZNote: Its oocysts glow blue-green under UV light — which is exactly how a stool sample gives it away.

lifeCycleStages: Unsporulated oocyst (passed in stool, non-infective until it sporulates in the environment)
Intracellular development within small intestinal epithelium

habitat.hostAssociation: Humans appear to be the only known host
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Oocysts must sporulate in the environment (days to weeks, depending on conditions) before becoming infectious, so direct person-to-person transmission is unlikely
habitat.reservoir: Contaminated water and fresh produce (classically imported berries, herbs, and leafy greens)

microscopy.stain: Modified acid-fast stain of stool; UV fluorescence microscopy
microscopy.appearance: Oocysts are acid-fast variable (often appear as wrinkled, non-uniform spheres) and demonstrate blue-green autofluorescence under UV light, a distinguishing feature from Cryptosporidium

culture.growthCharacteristics: Diagnosis relies on stool microscopy/staining rather than culture

biochemicalTests.result: Increasingly used, more sensitive than microscopy alone

identificationClues: Spherical oocysts (~8-10 µm, larger than Cryptosporidium) on modified acid-fast stain of stool
Distinctive blue-green autofluorescence under ultraviolet microscopy
Prolonged, relapsing watery diarrhea, sometimes lasting weeks and fluctuating in severity
Classic outbreaks linked to imported fresh produce, especially raspberries, basil, and other leafy herbs

diseases: Cyclosporiasis — watery diarrhea, often prolonged or relapsing/remitting over weeks, with fatigue, anorexia, and weight loss; can be more severe and persistent in immunocompromised patients
virulenceFactors: Invasion and disruption of small intestinal epithelial cells, impairing normal absorption
clinicalImportance.transmission: Fecal-oral, primarily via contaminated food (especially imported fresh produce like berries, basil, and lettuce) or water; oocysts require time in the environment to sporulate and become infectious, making direct person-to-person spread unlikely
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: Recurrent source of seasonal foodborne outbreaks in North America and Europe, frequently traced to imported fresh produce from endemic regions
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Distinguishing Cyclospora from the smaller, similarly acid-fast Cryptosporidium relies on oocyst size and characteristic UV autofluorescence; PCR panels are increasingly used for more sensitive detection

examFacts.keyBiochemicalReaction: Not applicable — diagnosed by stool microscopy/PCR
examFacts.importantTest: Modified acid-fast stain with UV autofluorescence of stool
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: An acid-fast, UV-autofluorescent intestinal parasite classically linked to outbreaks from imported fresh produce, causing unusually prolonged/relapsing diarrhea
